newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan tries to defuse tension of "inhuman" attack.
newsitem.headline: Jordan tries to defuse tension of "inhuman" attack.

text.p: Jordan swiftly condemned the killing of seven Israeli schoolgirls by a Jordanian soldier on Thursday, trying to defuse tension already running high after bitter political exchanges this week.

King Hussein, who said on Tuesday Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the Middle East "towards an abyss of bloodshed", cut short a foreign tour and returned to Jordan, expressing "shock, pain and anger" at the attack.

Crown Prince Hassan, speaking at a hospital where more than 20 Jordanians gave blood to help treat the Israeli wounded, said the shooting was "a murderous act carried out by a Jordanian soldier on his own".
Asked if it would further strain ties with Israel, the prince said: "I don't want to read anything political into this. This was an act of inhumanity and an act of murder."
The shooting, which took place on Jordanian land leased to Israel under their 1994 peace treaty, was the most serious violence along the heavily guarded border for many years.
Some Israeli government ministers suggested a link between the king's warning, prompted by Netanyahu's plans to build Jewish housing in East Jerusalem, and Thursday's shooting.
"Perhaps the conclusion is the king must hold his tongue so that a soldier doesn't take his words to mean more than he intended," Israel's Education Minister Zvulun Hammer said.
But Jordanian officials said the attack was an isolated act. They said 150,000 Israeli tourists had visited the country in safety since the former foes opened their border crossings.
The two countries had set up a joint team to investigate the shooting, they added.

Prime Minister Abdul-Karim al-Kabariti condemned the shooting as a "heinous crime" and pledged the soldier, who was overpowered by other Jordanian soldiers and arrested, would be "prosecuted to the full extent of the law".

"I don't think anybody, Israel or Jordan, is interested in a major problem," said one political analyst who asked not to be named. "This is an isolated incident happening in an atmosphere which is very tense."

Since the signing of the treaty King Hussein has been regarded as the Arab leader closest to Israel. Even before the treaty the two countries cooperated closely in security along their joint border, diplomats say.

But the king spoke out in a letter to Netanyahu, made public on Tuesday, in which he said the Israeli plans to build Jewish homes around Jerusalem and limit its next West Bank withdrawal to just nine percent of the land made peace in the Middle East "appear more and more like a distant elusive mirage".
After King Hussein's letter was published, Jordan television gave prime air-time for two days running to opposition calls in parliament for the 1994 treaty to be abrogated.
Many Jordanians will see the king's message as prescient.

"There have been a lot of warnings that violence will take place and that tensions are rising," former Jordanian prime minister Taher al-Masri said. "This shows just how angry people are over the developments in Jerusalem and the West Bank."
But Masri said both Israel and Jordan would try to dampen anger among their populations.
"Definitely they will try to overcome this. I think both sides will do something," he said.
